Dataset Attribute Information:¶

  1. age (age)
  2. sex (sex)
  3. chest pain type (4 values) (cp)
  4. resting blood pressure (trestbps)
  5. serum cholestoral in mg/dl (chol)
  6. fasting blood sugar > 120 mg/dl (fbs)
  7. resting electrocardiographic results (values 0,1,2) (restecg)
  8. maximum heart rate achieved (thalach)
  9. exercise induced angina (exang)
  10. oldpeak = ST depression induced by exercise relative to rest (oldpeak)
  11. the slope of the peak exercise ST segment (slope)
  12. number of major vessels (0-3) colored by flourosopy (ca)
  13. thal: 0 = normal; 1 = fixed defect; 2 = reversable defect (thal)

1.3 Key EDA Observations¶

Continuous Features:

  • thalach (max heart rate): Highest positive correlation with target. Patients with heart disease tend to have higher max heart rates
  • oldpeak (ST depression): Negative correlation with target. Lower oldpeak (< 1.0) is associated with higher probability of heart disease
  • age: Older patients show slightly higher disease risk, but it's not the strongest predictor
  • chol (cholesterol): Surprisingly weak correlation with target — not a strong standalone predictor

Categorical Features:

  • cp (chest pain type): Strong differentiator — type 2 is heavily associated with heart disease
  • thal: Values of 2 (reversible defect) strongly indicate heart disease; value 3 (normal) indicates no disease
  • ca (number of major vessels): ca=0 strongly associated with heart disease
  • exang (exercise-induced angina): exang=0 (no angina) is more common in heart disease patients
  • sex: More males in the dataset — potential source of bias (we'll discuss in Part 5)

Dataset Balance: ~54% positive / ~46% negative — reasonably balanced, so accuracy is a fair evaluation metric.

for col in continuous:
    Q1 = df[col].quantile(0.25)
    Q3 = df[col].quantile(0.75)
    IQR = Q3 - Q1
    lower = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
    upper = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
    outliers = df[(df[col] < lower) | (df[col] > upper)]
    print(f"{col}: {len(outliers)} outliers (range: {lower:.1f} - {upper:.1f})")

Outlier Handling Decision¶

Outliers detected (IQR method): trestbps (9), chol (5), oldpeak (5), thalach (1), age (0).

Decision: Keep outliers. With only 302 samples, removing outliers would lose too much data. These values may be medically valid (e.g., high blood pressure patients). StandardScaler will handle the scale differences, and neural networks are generally robust to moderate outliers.

Part 2: Neural Network from Scratch (NumPy)¶

2.1 Helper Functions¶

In [16]:
# Sigmoid activation function
def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-np.clip(z, -500, 500)))
    # np.exp(1000)  # gives overflow error, hence we clip z to prevent it


# Derivative of sigmoid (needed for backpropagation)
def sigmoid_derivative(a):
    return a * (1 - a)

# Binary cross-entropy loss
def binary_cross_entropy(y_true, y_pred):
    epsilon = 1e-8  # avoid log(0)
    y_pred = np.clip(y_pred, epsilon, 1 - epsilon)
    return -np.mean(y_true * np.log(y_pred) + (1 - y_true) * np.log(1 - y_pred))

2.2 Neural Network Class¶

In [17]:
class NeuralNetworkFromScratch:
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size, output_size, learning_rate=0.01):
        # Initialize weights randomly (small values) and biases as zeros
        np.random.seed(42)
        self.W1 = np.random.randn(input_size, hidden_size) * 0.01
        self.b1 = np.zeros((1, hidden_size))
        self.W2 = np.random.randn(hidden_size, output_size) * 0.01
        self.b2 = np.zeros((1, output_size))
        self.lr = learning_rate
        self.losses = []

    def forward(self, X):
        """Forward propagation: Input → Hidden → Output"""
        self.Z1 = X @ self.W1 + self.b1           # weighted sum (hidden)
        self.A1 = sigmoid(self.Z1)                  # activation (hidden)
        self.Z2 = self.A1 @ self.W2 + self.b2      # weighted sum (output)
        self.A2 = sigmoid(self.Z2)                  # prediction (output)
        return self.A2

    def backward(self, X, y):
        """Backpropagation: compute gradients"""
        m = X.shape[0]  # number of samples
        y = y.reshape(-1, 1)

        # Output layer gradients
        dZ2 = self.A2 - y                                    # error at output
        dW2 = (self.A1.T @ dZ2) / m                          # gradient for W2
        db2 = np.sum(dZ2, axis=0, keepdims=True) / m         # gradient for b2

        # Hidden layer gradients
        dZ1 = (dZ2 @ self.W2.T) * sigmoid_derivative(self.A1)  # error at hidden
        dW1 = (X.T @ dZ1) / m                                   # gradient for W1
        db1 = np.sum(dZ1, axis=0, keepdims=True) / m            # gradient for b1

        # Update weights and biases (gradient descent)
        self.W2 -= self.lr * dW2
        self.b2 -= self.lr * db2
        self.W1 -= self.lr * dW1
        self.b1 -= self.lr * db1

    def train(self, X, y, epochs=200, X_val=None, y_val=None):
        """Training loop"""
        self.val_losses = []
        for epoch in range(epochs):
            # Forward pass
            predictions = self.forward(X)

            # Compute loss
            loss = binary_cross_entropy(y.reshape(-1, 1), predictions)
            self.losses.append(loss)

            # Validation loss
            if X_val is not None:
                val_pred = self.forward(X_val)
                val_loss = binary_cross_entropy(y_val.reshape(-1, 1), val_pred)
                self.val_losses.append(val_loss)
                self.forward(X)  # re-run forward on train to restore activations

            # Backward pass
            self.backward(X, y)

            # Print progress every 50 epochs
            if (epoch + 1) % 50 == 0:
                val_str = f", Val Loss: {val_loss:.4f}" if X_val is not None else ""
                print(f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{epochs} - Loss: {loss:.4f}{val_str}")

    def predict(self, X):
        """Make predictions (0 or 1)"""
        probabilities = self.forward(X)
        return (probabilities >= 0.5).astype(int).flatten()

2.4 Improved Training (Higher Learning Rate & More Epochs)¶

The first model did not learn properly — loss was stuck near 0.693 which means it was just guessing randomly. The learning rate of 0.01 was too small and 200 epochs was not enough. So I increased the learning rate to 0.1 and trained for 1000 epochs.

    'Sigmoid + SGD':  {'activation': 'sigmoid', 'optimizer': tf.keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=0.1)},

    'Sigmoid + Adam': {'activation': 'sigmoid', 'optimizer': tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.001)},
    'ReLU + Adam':    {'activation': 'relu',    'optimizer': tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.001)},
}

results = {}

for name, config in experiments.items():
    tf.random.set_seed(42)
    model = Sequential([
        Dense(8, activation=config['activation'], input_shape=(13,)),
        Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')
    ])
    model.compile(optimizer=config['optimizer'], loss='binary_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])
    
    history = model.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train_np,
                        validation_data=(X_val_scaled, y_val_np),
                        epochs=200, batch_size=32, verbose=0)
    
    test_loss, test_acc = model.evaluate(X_test_scaled, y_test_np, verbose=0)
    val_acc = model.evaluate(X_val_scaled, y_val_np, verbose=0)[1]
    train_acc = model.evaluate(X_train_scaled, y_train_np, verbose=0)[1]
    
    results[name] = {
        'Train Acc': train_acc,
        'Val Acc': val_acc,
        'Test Acc': test_acc,
        'history': history
    }
    print(f"{name:<20} → Train: {train_acc:.4f}  Val: {val_acc:.4f}  Test: {test_acc:.4f}")

3.3 Best Model Evaluation¶

Sigmoid + Adam and ReLU + Adam both gave the best test accuracy of 78.3%. I chose Sigmoid + Adam since it matches our scratch implementation. ReLU + SGD had the highest training accuracy (96.7%) but worst test accuracy (69.6%), which means it was overfitting badly. Adam optimizer worked better than SGD for both activations.

4.3 Hyperparameter Analysis Findings¶

Learning Rate:

  • LR=0.0001 gave the best test accuracy (84.8%) even though it had the lowest training accuracy (71.1%). This shows it was not overfitting and was generalizing well to new data.
  • Higher learning rates like 0.1 reached 100% on training data but only 78.3% on test data, which is a clear sign of overfitting.

Architecture:

  • All single layer models (4, 8, and 16 neurons) gave the same test accuracy of 78.3%.
  • Adding more layers actually made things worse — 2 layers gave 76% and 3 layers gave only 73.9% on test data.
  • This makes sense because with only 302 samples, bigger models start memorizing the data instead of learning useful patterns.

Best configuration: LR=0.0001 with a single hidden layer of 8 neurons gave the best balance of learning and generalization.

Part 5: Written Analysis & Reflection¶

In this case study, I built a neural network from scratch using NumPy to predict heart disease, and then recreated the same using Keras. The scratch implementation had 13 input features, 8 hidden neurons with sigmoid activation, and 1 output neuron. My first attempt with learning rate 0.01 and 200 epochs did not work at all — the model was just guessing randomly with 54% accuracy. After increasing the learning rate to 0.1 and training for 1000 epochs, the accuracy improved to 76% on test data. In Keras, I tried different activations and optimizers and found that Sigmoid with Adam optimizer gave the best test accuracy of 78.3%.

One ethical concern I noticed is the gender imbalance in the dataset. There are many more male patients than female patients. Since this is a medical dataset, this is a serious issue. Heart disease in women is already underdiagnosed in real life, and if our model has mostly learned from male patient data, it may not predict correctly for female patients. Wrong predictions in healthcare can have very dangerous consequences.

My preprocessing choices also affect this problem. I used StandardScaler on all data together without checking if male and female patients have different feature distributions. Also, when I did the train/test split, I used stratify on the target variable but did not check if both genders were equally represented in each split. So the model may have learned patterns that work better for one gender.

To reduce this risk, one simple step would be to check the model accuracy separately for male and female patients. If there is a big gap, we can try collecting more female patient data, or use techniques like oversampling to balance the gender representation in our training set.

The biggest learning from this case study is that tuning hyperparameters matters a lot. A wrong learning rate can make the model completely useless. I also learned that deeper and bigger networks are not always better — on small datasets like this one (only 302 samples), simple models actually perform better because complex models tend to memorize the training data instead of learning general patterns. Building the network from scratch really helped me understand what is happening inside forward propagation and backpropagation, which Keras hides from us.
